A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Representation Unlearning framework. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching retained appendices A–F and identifying the new Appendix G.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-data experiments, class and random unlearning benchmarks, computational measurements, and hyperparameter analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluated baselines, Neural Collapse diagnostics, and experiments perturbing zero-shot proxies.

M1.justification: Algorithm 2 changes zero-shot retention weighting from the global class prior p(y=c) to the retain prior p(yr=c), adding its calculation. This corrects the pseudocode to match Equation 10 already present in v1; the architecture and main-text objectives remain unchanged, and an implementation change is not established.

E1.justification: Both versions use the six-class synthetic dataset, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet for the same class and random unlearning tasks. Appendix G perturbs internal proxy weights within this coverage; it introduces no new dataset, population, or input domain. LLM applications remain future work.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 add evaluated Pretrained, Langevin Unlearning, AMUN, and NatMU comparators. Figures 4 and 6 also add the three new unlearning methods to efficiency comparisons. This substantially broadens the comparison set; the existing zero-shot comparators remain.

E3.justification: Section 4.3 and Table 2 replace the reported MIA privacy evaluation with RMIA. Appendix G introduces Neural Collapse diagnostics and a Gaussian proxy-noise protocol with sigma values 0, 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3. Existing dataset/model assignments and forget fractions remain unchanged; Appendix F still uses its original MIA AUC evaluation.

E4.justification: New Appendix G tests the central zero-shot proxy assumption using NC1, NC3, NC4, and classifier-versus-prototype accuracy gaps, then measures sensitivity to corrupted proxies in both unlearning tasks. These add substantial assumption-validation and robustness evidence beyond the unchanged beta/depth analyses in Section 4.5 and Appendix F.

E5.justification: v1 already reports plus/minus values but does not identify their meaning or benchmark run count. v2 specifies means and standard deviations across five random seeds, with fixed forgotten classes and different random-unlearning splits per seed. This is newly disclosed statistical information, not evidence that the number of runs increased.

E6.justification: Existing results change substantially: Table 1 revises SISA's Tiny ImageNet retain accuracy, forget accuracy, and CE from 58.9%, 58.2%, and 1.87 to 50.2%, 0.0%, and 3.05. Table 2 replaces privacy scores under RMIA, while Figure 4 revises reported speed-ups. New comparator rows, inference-overhead measurements, and Tables 12–14 add further results. Privacy scores across versions use different attacks and do not establish same-setting gains.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, variational bounds, assumptions used in their derivations, and Appendix A proofs are unchanged. Algorithm 2 aligns its weighting with an existing equation; Appendix G supplies empirical diagnostics and interpretations rather than new formal bounds or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same core contributions: representation-space information compression, standard and zero-shot regimes, and claimed utility and efficiency advantages. The conclusion's maximum speed-up changes from 754× to 757×, a numerical update without a substantive change in the claim.

C2.justification: New Section 5 explicitly restricts protection to black-box access, acknowledges recoverable information in the frozen encoder, and discusses permanent inference overhead and dependence on Neural Collapse. Appendix G interprets proxy degradation as a privacy–utility trade-off. Section 4.3 also replaces the interpretation that SISA fails to forget with successful forgetting constrained by retraining costs.

D1.justification: v2 adds split-selection details, specifies Gaussian corruption of proxy weights, and reports transformation inference overheads of 0.59 microseconds on CIFAR-10 and 1.09 on Tiny ImageNet. Existing hyperparameter Tables 3–11 and code-access information remain unchanged; corresponding settings for the newly added baselines and RMIA are not supplied.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantive positioning against concept erasure and representation-editing research, including LEACE, kernelized rate-distortion, domain-adversarial representation erasure, and gradient-free forgetting. It distinguishes the proposed method through instance/class removal, tractable objectives, and zero-shot operation. The retain-access taxonomy also expands to incorporate Langevin, AMUN, and NatMU.

P1.justification: Related-work and results paragraphs receive targeted rewrites, and new Limitations and Future Directions sections precede the renumbered conclusion. Appendix G and an evaluation-protocol paragraph are added, and the publication header changes. Most introductory, methodological, and retained appendix prose remains unchanged.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 gain comparator rows, Figures 4 and 6 gain bars and revised ordering, and Appendix G adds Tables 12–14. Text and figure placement adjust to accommodate these additions. The overall visual design, conceptual figures, and existing sensitivity heatmaps are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in v1 by explicitly acknowledging white-box vulnerability and directly testing the Neural Collapse assumption underlying zero-shot unlearning. Broader comparisons and clarified uncertainty further improve assessability. Missing new-baseline/RMIA settings and overstated robustness language remain drawbacks: Table 13 shows Tiny ImageNet forget accuracy rising from 1.1% to 6.0% despite claiming unaffected forgetting. Nevertheless, the scope clarification and new assumption tests substantially improve the paper's overall evidential grounding.
